Master-ai formalizes the estimator itself (the ensemble-average formula f-hat_RF(x) = (1/N) sum_i T_i(x)); the course formalizes the variance effect (averaging B independent models of variance sigma^2 each reduces variance to sigma^2/B, with the caveat that correlated trees achieve less). Neither unit contains the other's claim: one defines the model, the other analyzes its variance. Both are needed for a complete treatment — the definition and the analysis — hence complementary content rather than partial overlap.
topic: Random Forest mathematical formalization (ensemble formula vs variance analysis)

rationale: The two vaults (and master-ai internally) date XGBoost differently, and the difference is a genuine historical distinction rather than an error on one side: master-ai's implementation list says 'XGBoost (2014)' while its own Further Reading cites 'Chen & Guestrin (2016), XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System'; the course frames XGBoost as 'the dominant library from 2016 to 2019'. Historically, both dates label real events: the XGBoost library was first released in March 2014 (master-ai's '(2014)' plausibly refers to the library), while the paper by Chen & Guestrin is arXiv:1603.02754 (submitted March 2016) and was published at KDD 2016 — so master-ai mixes a library-release year with a paper-publication year without distinguishing them (internally inconsistent within one note). Synthesis must reconcile explicitly — recommended: cite Chen & Guestrin (2016, KDD; arXiv March 2016; library first released 2014) — rather than silently picking one vault's year. Term-evidence note: the course's section heading also dates the library '(Chen and Guestrin, 2016)', but headings are outside KU excerpts, so the course-side evidence here is the dominance-era claim.
topic: XGBoost era dating (2014 vs 2016)
